reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: Renal amyloidosis is caused by deposition of misfolded protein as insoluble beta-pleated fibrils, most often AL (monoclonal light chain) or AA (serum amyloid A in chronic inflammation)
Presents typically with heavy proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome, often with preserved-sized or enlarged kidneys despite renal impairment
Congo-red staining showing apple-green birefringence under polarised light is the diagnostic hallmark on biopsy
Amyloid typing (by mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry) is essential because AL, AA and hereditary forms have entirely different treatments
AL amyloidosis reflects an underlying plasma-cell clone and demands a paraprotein and free light-chain workup with cardiac assessment
AA amyloidosis follows chronic inflammatory, infective or autoinflammatory disease, so control of the underlying inflammation is central
Management is directed at the source: clone-directed therapy for paraprotein-related AL disease and suppression of inflammation for AA disease
reference.pathophysiology: Amyloidosis is a disorder of protein misfolding in which a precursor protein aggregates into stable, insoluble beta-pleated sheet fibrils that deposit in the extracellular matrix. In AL amyloidosis a clonal plasma-cell population produces monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains prone to misfolding; in AA amyloidosis the acute-phase reactant serum amyloid A is overproduced during chronic inflammation and its cleavage fragments deposit. In the kidney, fibrils accumulate preferentially in the mesangium and glomerular basement membrane, and later in vessel walls and the interstitium, expanding the mesangium and disrupting the filtration barrier to cause progressive proteinuria and renal impairment. The Congo-red-positive deposits are non-branching fibrils on electron microscopy.
additionalDifferentials: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with heavy proteinuria
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy with Congo-red staining and polarised microscopy
Amyloid typing by mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with serum free light chains
Bone marrow examination for a plasma-cell clone in suspected AL disease
Cardiac assessment (echocardiography, biomarkers) and search for other organ involvement
Screening for chronic inflammatory or infective disease and SAA levels in suspected AA disease
redFlags: Cardiac involvement with heart failure or arrhythmia, a major determinant of survival in AL disease
Rapidly worsening renal function or profound nephrotic syndrome
Newly identified monoclonal protein or plasma-cell dyscrasia
Autonomic dysfunction, gastrointestinal bleeding or bleeding diathesis suggesting multisystem amyloid
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends chiefly on amyloid type and extra-renal involvement, particularly the heart in AL disease, which dominates survival. Reducing the amyloidogenic precursor, whether by clone-directed therapy in AL disease or by controlling inflammation in AA disease, can stabilise or improve organ function, but advanced renal or cardiac deposition carries a poor outlook.
pitfalls: Failing to type the amyloid, leading to inappropriate treatment
Assuming small kidneys, when amyloid kidneys are often normal or enlarged
Overlooking cardiac involvement that governs prognosis in AL disease
Not screening for an underlying plasma-cell clone or chronic inflammatory driver
Attributing nodular glomerular lesions to diabetes without Congo-red staining
management: Establish the amyloid type by tissue typing before treatment, as AL, AA and hereditary forms require entirely different therapy
Treat AL disease with clone-directed therapy against the plasma-cell clone, such as bortezomib-based regimens with daratumumab, to reduce the amyloidogenic light chain

Treat AA disease by suppressing the underlying inflammation, using targeted biologics such as interleukin-1 or tumour necrosis factor inhibitors where an autoinflammatory or rheumatic driver is present
Manage the nephrotic syndrome with renin-angiotensin blockade to reduce proteinuria, and diuretics with salt restriction for oedema
Monitor renal function, proteinuria and cardiac involvement, and address the thrombotic risk of heavy proteinuria
Provide renal replacement therapy for progressive failure and consider transplantation once the precursor is controlled
Manage jointly with nephrology, haematology and cardiology, and arrange genetic counselling if a hereditary form is confirmed
